blocks.html: In a wire, electrons can move freely from atom to atom. Connect the wire to a battery and they flow. Two numbers describe this flow: how much charge passes each second, and how much energy each bit of charge carries.

Current $I$ is the rate of flow of charge: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$, in amperes (A), where 1 A is 1 coulomb per second. Voltage $V$ is the energy given to each coulomb of charge, in volts (V), where 1 V is 1 joule per coulomb.

Think of a loop of water pipe with a pump. The pump (the battery) gives the water energy; the flow rate (the current) is how much water passes a point each second. In a light bulb the charge gives up its energy as light and heat, but the charge itself keeps going around the loop: what goes into the bulb comes out of it. Current is not used up; energy is transferred.

blocks.name: ph-circuit
blocks.cap: A 6 V battery, an ammeter and a bulb. The moving dots show the current. It is the same all the way around the loop.

blocks.title: Find the current
blocks.q: 30 coulombs of charge flow through a lamp in 10 s. What is the current?
steps: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t} = \dfrac{30\,\mathrm{C}}{10\,\mathrm{s}} = 3\,\mathrm{A}$.

blocks.title: Energy from voltage
blocks.q: A 9 V battery pushes 4 C of charge through a circuit. How much energy does it give the charge?
steps: Each coulomb gets 9 J.
$4 \times 9 = 36$ J.

blocks.html: Thinking current gets used up as it passes through a bulb, so less comes out than goes in. An ammeter placed before the bulb and one placed after read the same. What the bulb uses is energy, carried by the charge; the charge itself returns to the battery.

The electrons in a wire drift along slowly, often less than a millimeter per second. A lamp still lights almost at once, because the wire is already full of electrons and they all start moving together, like water in a full hose.

blocks.html: A current needs a complete path. A battery pushes charge out of one terminal, and that charge must be able to travel all the way around and back into the other terminal. Such a closed path is a circuit.

Charge flows only around a closed loop from one terminal of the battery, through the devices, back to the other terminal. A gap anywhere (an open circuit) stops the current everywhere in that loop. A switch is a gap you can open and close.

The battery doesn't supply charges; the wires are already full of them. It pushes them around the loop, like a pump pushing water around a closed pipe. Break the pipe anywhere and the whole flow stops, because the water has nowhere to go. That is why one switch by the door can turn off a light across the room.

blocks.name: ph-circuit
blocks.cap: Two bulbs and a switch in one loop. Click the switch to open it: both bulbs go out, because the loop is broken.

blocks.title: Does it light?
blocks.q: A bulb has two connection points. One wire joins it to the + terminal of a battery. Nothing is connected to its other point. Does it light?
steps: For current, charge must go from one terminal, through the bulb, and back to the other terminal.
Here there is no path back to the battery, so there is no loop.

blocks.title: Where the switch goes
blocks.q: Two bulbs are wired in one loop with a battery and a switch. The switch is opened. Which bulbs go out?
steps: All the parts share the same single loop.
Opening the switch breaks that loop, so the current stops everywhere in it.

blocks.html: Connecting a bulb to only one end of a battery and expecting it to light. Charge must leave the battery, pass through the bulb and return, so the bulb needs two connections: one to each terminal (directly or through other parts).

blocks.html: Push harder and more current flows; put something in the way and less flows. The "something in the way" is resistance. A bulb filament or a resistor resists the flow, turning electrical energy into heat and light. Solving the law is a one-step equation, in any complete circuit.
Ohm's law: $$V = I\,R$$ Voltage (V) = current (A) × resistance in ohms (Ω). So $I = \dfrac{V}{R}$ and $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$.

For many materials, doubling the voltage doubles the current: current and voltage are proportional. The resistance is the constant ratio $\dfrac{V}{I}$, a property of the resistor itself, set by its material, length and thickness. A thin, long wire has more resistance than a short, thick one, just as a narrow pipe lets less water through.

blocks.name: ph-circuit
blocks.cap: A 12 V battery and a 4 Ω resistor: the ammeter reads 3 A. Click the resistor to change its resistance and watch the current change.

blocks.title: Find the current
blocks.q: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor. Find the current.
steps: $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{12\,\mathrm{V}}{4\,\Omega} = 3\,\mathrm{A}$.

blocks.title: Find the resistance
blocks.q: A lamp draws 0.5 A from a 6 V supply. What is its resistance?
steps: $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{6\,\mathrm{V}}{0.5\,\mathrm{A}} = 12\,\Omega$.

blocks.html: Thinking a resistor's resistance changes when the current through it changes. For an ordinary resistor, if you double the voltage, the current doubles too, and $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$ stays the same. Resistance depends on the resistor, not on what you connect it to. (A bulb filament is an exception in one way: its resistance rises as it heats up.)
Measure currents and voltages yourself in the Circuit Builder.

blocks.html: With two or more parts in a circuit, you can connect them in a line (series) or side by side on separate branches (parallel). The two ways behave very differently, and Ohm's law explains how.

Series: one path, so the same current flows through every part; resistances add, $R = R_1 + R_2$, and the battery's voltage is shared among the parts. Parallel: each branch connects straight across the battery, so each gets the full voltage; the branch currents add up to the total.

In series, every charge must pass through every part in turn, so the current can't differ from one part to the next, and each added part makes the path harder. In parallel, each branch is its own loop through the battery. Adding a branch adds another path, so the battery delivers more total current, and removing one branch leaves the others working. That is why homes are wired in parallel.

blocks.name: ph-circuit
blocks.cap: One bulb in series with two in parallel. Bulb B1 carries the whole current, so it glows brightest. Click a bulb to remove it and see what happens to the others.

blocks.title: Series
blocks.q: A 12 V battery is connected to a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor in series. Find the current and the voltage across each resistor.
steps: Total resistance: $2 + 4 = 6\,\Omega$.
Current: $I = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2$ A, the same through both.
Voltages: $2 \times 2 = 4$ V and $2 \times 4 = 8$ V. They add to 12 V.

blocks.title: Parallel
blocks.q: The same resistors are connected in parallel to the 12 V battery. Find the current in each and the total current.
steps: Each branch gets the full 12 V.
Total from the battery: $6 + 3 = 9$ A.

blocks.html: Thinking the first bulb in a series circuit is brightest because it gets the current first. The current is the same everywhere in a series loop at the same moment, so identical bulbs in series glow equally. Check: there is nowhere for current to "leak" out between the bulbs.
Try series and parallel bulbs in the Circuit Builder.

blocks.html: A lamp, a toaster and a TV all turn electrical energy into other forms, at different rates. That rate is power, and for electricity it comes straight from current and voltage.
Electric power: $$P = V\,I$$ in watts. Energy used = power × time. Power companies count energy in kilowatt-hours (kWh): 1 kWh is the energy a 1,000 W device uses in 1 hour.

Voltage is joules per coulomb, and current is coulombs per second. Multiply them and the coulombs cancel: (J/C) × (C/s) = J/s = watts. A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power: $1\,\mathrm{kW} \times 1\,\mathrm{h} = 1{,}000\,\mathrm{J/s} \times 3{,}600\,\mathrm{s} = 3{,}600{,}000\,\mathrm{J}$.

blocks.name: ph-circuit
blocks.cap: Two bulbs in parallel on 12 V. The one with less resistance draws more current, so it uses more power and glows brighter.

blocks.title: Power from current and voltage
blocks.q: A hair dryer draws 10 A from a 120 V outlet. What is its power?
steps: $P = V\,I = 120\,\mathrm{V} \times 10\,\mathrm{A} = 1{,}200\,\mathrm{W} = 1.2\,\mathrm{kW}$.

blocks.title: The cost of energy
blocks.q: A 1.5 kW space heater runs for 4 hours. Electricity costs 15 cents per kWh. How much energy does it use, and what does it cost?
steps: Energy: $1.5\,\mathrm{kW} \times 4\,\mathrm{h} = 6\,\mathrm{kWh}$.
Cost: $6 \times 15 = 90$ cents.

blocks.html: Mixing up kilowatts (a rate) with kilowatt-hours (an amount of energy). A 2 kW kettle uses energy at 2 kW whether it runs for a minute or an hour; the kWh you pay for depend on how long it runs. Check the units: kW × h = kWh.

blocks.html: A magnet pulls on iron from a distance through its field. Every magnet has two ends where its pull is strongest, called poles, and the rules for poles look a lot like the rules for charges.

Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Outside the magnet, its field lines run from the north pole to the south pole, and a compass needle lines up along them.

A magnet is made of countless tiny magnets: in iron, many of the atoms behave like little magnets, and in a magnet they are lined up. Cut a bar magnet in half and each half still has its tiny magnets lined up, so each half is a whole magnet with its own north and south pole. No one has ever found a north pole by itself.

blocks.cap: A bar magnet's field, shown by lines and compass needles. Break the magnet and each piece has both poles.

blocks.title: Attract or repel?
blocks.q: The north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another. What happens?
steps: North and south are unlike poles.
Unlike poles attract.

blocks.title: Earth as a magnet
blocks.q: A compass needle's north pole points toward Earth's Arctic. What kind of magnetic pole is near the Arctic?
steps: The needle's north pole is attracted there.
Unlike poles attract, so the magnetic pole near the Arctic is a south magnetic pole, even though we call that region "north."

blocks.html: Thinking that breaking a magnet in half separates its north pole from its south pole. Each piece becomes a complete magnet with both poles, however small you cut it. Check: test each piece's ends with a compass.

blocks.html: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed a compass needle twitch when he switched on a current nearby. Electricity and magnetism turned out to be linked: every current makes a magnetic field.

An electric current makes a magnetic field around it. Wind the wire into a coil and the fields add up, giving a field like a bar magnet's. Put an iron core inside and the field becomes much stronger: an electromagnet, which you can switch on and off.

Around a straight wire, the field forms circles. In a coil, the circles from every loop point the same way through the middle, so they add: more turns or more current make a stronger magnet. The iron core's own tiny magnets line up with the coil's field and add their much larger field. Switch off the current and the field disappears, which is why a scrapyard crane can drop what it picked up.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: A coil around an iron core. With current flowing, it has a north and a south pole like a bar magnet.

blocks.title: Make it stronger
blocks.q: Name three ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
steps: Increase the current through the coil.
Wind more turns of wire.
Use an iron core.
blocks.a: More current, more turns, an iron core

blocks.html: An electric motor puts this to work: a magnetic field pushes on a current-carrying coil, making it spin. That turns electrical energy into motion in fans, drills and electric cars.

blocks.cap: A simple motor: the magnetic force on the current in the loop turns it.

blocks.html: Thinking only permanent magnets make magnetic fields. Any electric current does, which is how an electromagnet works with no magnet inside it at all. Check: reverse the current and the electromagnet's poles swap.

blocks.html: If a current can make a magnetic field (an electromagnet), can a magnet make a current? In 1831 Michael Faraday found that it can, but only while something is changing. That discovery runs almost every power plant in the world.

Moving a magnet near a coil, or a coil near a magnet, induces a current in the coil. The current flows only while the magnetic field through the coil is changing. Faster motion, a stronger magnet or more turns make a bigger current. A generator uses this to turn motion into electrical energy.

Push a magnet into a coil and the field inside the coil grows, so a current flows. Hold it still and nothing changes, so the current stops. Pull it out and the current flows the other way. In a generator, a coil spins between magnets, so the field through it changes all the time, and by conservation of energy, the electrical energy comes from the work done turning the coil.

blocks.title: Magnet and coil
blocks.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil, held still inside it, then pulled out. When does the meter show a current?
steps: Pushing in: the field in the coil grows, so a current flows.
Held still: no change, no current.
Pulling out: the field shrinks, so a current flows the other way.
blocks.a: Only while the magnet moves; opposite ways in and out

blocks.title: Where the energy comes from
blocks.q: A wind turbine's blades turn a generator. What energy change happens?
steps: The wind's kinetic energy turns the blades.
The generator turns that motion into electrical energy (plus some heat).

blocks.html: Thinking a magnet resting inside a coil makes a steady current. A current is induced only while the field through the coil is changing. A still magnet gives a steady field and no current. Check: watch the meter while the magnet is still.
In most power plants, steam, falling water or wind spins a turbine connected to a generator. The current in your outlets swings back and forth 60 times each second (60 Hz) in North America.
